blocks.text: A 78-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his nephew, who manages his pension and answers every question for him. The patient has bruises on both upper arms, is underweight and wearing soiled clothes, and glances at his nephew before he speaks. Nothing he says is a complaint, yet the picture should make you think.

blocks.markdown: **Safeguarding** means protecting a person's right to live in safety, free from abuse and neglect. In England the Care Act 2014 places adult safeguarding duties on local authorities and expects every professional to recognise and report concern. This unit teaches you three skills: recognising the forms abuse takes, asking about domestic abuse safely, and deciding when confidentiality may lawfully be set aside.

blocks.title: Adult at risk
blocks.text: In the Care Act 2014 an adult at risk is a person aged 18 or over who (1) has needs for care and support, (2) is experiencing, or is at risk of, abuse or neglect, and (3) because of those needs is unable to protect themselves. Being old, disabled or unwell does not on its own make someone an adult at risk; all three conditions apply.

blocks.markdown: Abuse is rarely a single dramatic event. It is usually a pattern of behaviour by someone with power over the person: a relative, a paid carer, a partner or a care organisation. Risk factors include cognitive impairment, dependency on one carer, social isolation, carer stress, substance misuse by the abuser, and communication difficulty. The abuser is often someone the person loves or relies on, which is why the person may not disclose.

rows: Physical
Hitting, restraint, misuse of medication, rough handling
Bruises in unusual sites (e.g. inner arms, trunk), finger-mark bruising, unexplained fractures, over-sedation
Sexual
Any sexual act without valid consent, including with a person who lacks capacity
Genital or anal injury, sexually transmitted infection, sudden behavioural change
Psychological or emotional
Threats, humiliation, isolation, removal of choice
Fearfulness, withdrawal, deferring to a carer, low mood
Financial or material
Theft, fraud, pressure over wills or property, misuse of benefits
Unpaid bills despite adequate income, sudden changes to a will, a relative controlling money
Neglect and acts of omission
Failing to provide food, warmth, hygiene, medicines or care
Weight loss, pressure ulcers, poor hygiene, missed medication
Self-neglect
Person neglects own hygiene, health or surroundings
Hoarding, refusing needed care, unsafe home
Domestic abuse
Controlling, coercive or violent behaviour by a partner or family member
Repeated injuries, a partner who will not leave the room, delayed presentation
Organisational and discriminatory
Poor or abusive routines in a care setting; harassment based on protected characteristics
Institutional practices, rigid rules, group-wide neglect
blocks.caption: Forms of abuse recognised in Care Act statutory guidance (modern slavery is also listed there). Categories overlap.

blocks.title: Recognising abuse from a collateral picture
blocks.prompt: A district nurse visits a 84-year-old woman with dementia who lives with her daughter. The daughter says her mother 'refuses to eat'. The nurse finds a sacral pressure ulcer, a dry mouth, a house with no food in the kitchen, and a recent unexplained withdrawal of £3000 from the woman's savings. Which forms of abuse should be considered?

steps.text: List each finding and ask what harm it could represent. A sacral pressure ulcer and dry mouth suggest that basic care, repositioning and fluids have not been provided.
No food in the house and a dependent person losing weight points to neglect or an act of omission, even if unintentional because of carer stress.
A large unexplained withdrawal from the woman's savings, when she lacks capacity to manage money, raises financial abuse.

A person with dementia may not be able to describe what is happening, so concern is built from the whole picture and not from the patient's account alone. No single finding proves abuse, but together they meet the threshold to share concern.

blocks.answer: Neglect (acts of omission) and possible financial abuse; this is a safeguarding concern to be escalated to the local authority adult safeguarding team through your organisation's route, not something to investigate alone.

blocks.markdown:
### Asking about domestic abuse

Domestic abuse covers controlling, coercive, threatening or violent behaviour between people who are, or have been, intimate partners or family members. Many patients will not volunteer it, but most say they would like to be asked sensitively. Three conditions make enquiry safe:

1. **Privacy.** Speak to the patient alone. Create a routine reason to separate them from a partner or relative, such as 'I need to examine you / do the next part of the assessment on your own'. Never ask in front of a partner, a family member or a child old enough to repeat it.
2. **Interpreters.** Use a professional interpreter. Never use a relative or friend to interpret.
3. **Approach.** Start from the symptoms or context, use open, non-judgemental questions, and normalise: 'Because abuse is common and affects health, I ask everyone...'. Believe the patient and avoid blaming language.

items: Find a way to see the patient on their own and explain that what is said is confidential, with the limits of that confidentiality.
Introduce the question with a reason: 'Many people I see are frightened of someone at home, so I ask everyone.'
Ask directly but gently, for example 'Has anyone hurt you or made you afraid?'
If they disclose: listen, validate ('this is not your fault'), ask about immediate safety, and offer specialist support and referral.
Record what was said factually, and in a place where an abuser cannot see it.

blocks.title: Do not confront the suspected abuser
blocks.text: Do not tell a partner or carer that you suspect abuse, do not post letters or text messages to the patient's home without agreement, and do not leave leaflets in view. Any of these can increase danger to the patient. Safe contact methods are agreed with the patient.

blocks.markdown:
### Confidentiality and when it may be breached

Confidentiality is a core duty, but it is not absolute. The GMC's confidentiality guidance sets out the principles you apply:

- **Consent first.** Where an adult has capacity, the starting point is to seek their consent to share information, and to respect a refusal. An adult with capacity may choose to stay in a risky situation.
- **Required by law or court order.** Disclose when the law requires it.
- **Public interest.** Disclosure without consent may be justified where it is necessary to protect an individual or society from a risk of death or serious harm, for example a serious crime, or where others (including children in the household) are at risk.
- **Lack of capacity.** If the adult lacks capacity to decide, under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 you act in their **best interests**, which can include sharing information with those who need to know.
- **Proportionality.** Share the minimum necessary, only with those who need it, and record your reasoning. Tell the patient before disclosing unless doing so would put them or others at greater risk.

blocks.title: Weighing confidentiality against risk
blocks.prompt: A 45-year-old woman with capacity attends her GP with a fractured wrist. In private she says her husband pushed her down the stairs, that he has done this before, and that she does not want anyone told. Her two young children are at home with him. What should the doctor do about confidentiality?

steps.text: Establish capacity: she is making a decision about her own information and has capacity, so her refusal carries weight. Explore her reasons and offer support, risk assessment and referral to specialist domestic abuse services.

Ask whether the risk extends to others. Young children living with a perpetrator of repeated violence are potentially at risk of serious harm, which changes the analysis from her own choice to protection of children.

Where a child may be at risk of serious harm, the public interest in protecting them can justify sharing information without her consent. Tell her first if safe, share only what is needed with the appropriate children's safeguarding route, and document the reasoning.
If there were no children and no one else at risk, her capacitous refusal would normally be respected, with the door left open and safety planning offered.

blocks.answer: Respect her refusal about her own care where she has capacity, but share the minimum necessary information with the safeguarding route because the children may be at risk of serious harm; document the decision and reasons.

blocks.title: Role of the student and junior doctor
blocks.text: You are not expected to investigate or prove abuse. You are expected to recognise warning signs, respond kindly, record facts, and escalate promptly to your supervisor and the named safeguarding lead, following local policy. If you are unsure, discuss with someone senior; never carry a concern alone.

points: An adult at risk has care and support needs, is experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, and cannot protect themselves because of those needs.
Abuse takes many overlapping forms including physical, sexual, psychological, financial, neglect, self-neglect, domestic and organisational abuse.
Ask about domestic abuse alone, with a professional interpreter if needed, using open, non-judgemental questions, and record safely.

Confidentiality may be breached with consent, by law, in the public interest to prevent serious harm, or in the best interests of a person lacking capacity, sharing the minimum necessary and documenting why.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with moderate learning disability lives in a residential home. Staff routinely lock her in her room for hours because 'she is easier to manage'. Which form of abuse does this best represent?

options.text: Organisational abuse and restriction of liberty
Financial abuse
Self-neglect
Domestic abuse by a partner

questions.correctOptionText: Organisational abuse and restriction of liberty

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the routine is a care-setting practice that restricts liberty for staff convenience.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: no money or property is involved.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: self-neglect is the person neglecting their own care, not others restricting her.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the abusers are care staff, not an intimate partner or family member.

questions.explanation: Abusive practices built into the routines of a care setting are organisational abuse, and locking someone away also deprives them of liberty. Safeguarding concerns like this should be raised with the local authority safeguarding team and the home's regulator.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a recommended approach when you suspect a patient is experiencing domestic abuse?

options.text: Ask the patient alone and use a professional interpreter if needed
Ask with the partner present so he or she can respond
Use the patient's adult son as interpreter to save time
Wait for the patient to raise the subject before asking anything

questions.correctOptionText: Ask the patient alone and use a professional interpreter if needed

distractorRationale.a: Correct: privacy and an independent interpreter are the minimum conditions for safe enquiry.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: a partner who is the abuser may retaliate and the patient cannot answer freely.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: family members must not interpret because they may be involved or may disclose to the abuser.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: many patients will not volunteer abuse but would welcome sensitive enquiry.

questions.explanation: Safe enquiry requires privacy and an interpreter who has no link to the family. Asking in front of the partner or through a relative can put the patient at greater risk and prevent honest disclosure.

questions.stem: An older adult is automatically an 'adult at risk' under the Care Act 2014 solely because of their age.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: An adult at risk must have care and support needs, be at risk of abuse or neglect, and be unable to protect themselves because of those needs. Age alone does not meet these conditions.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man with capacity tells you in private that his partner hits him. He asks you not to tell anyone, and no children or other adults are at risk. What is the most appropriate approach to confidentiality?

options.text: Respect his decision, offer support and specialist services, and keep the offer open
Inform the police immediately without telling him
Phone his partner to ask for an explanation
Tell his employer so that he can be protected at work

questions.correctOptionText: Respect his decision, offer support and specialist services, and keep the offer open

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a capacitous adult may refuse disclosure where no one else is at risk of serious harm.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: no legal duty or overriding public interest has been identified and he refused.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: contacting the abuser could escalate danger.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: an employer has no need to know and disclosure would be disproportionate.

questions.explanation: With capacity and no risk to others, the adult's refusal is normally respected, and you continue to offer support, safety planning and access to specialist services. Disclosure without consent needs a clear legal or public interest justification such as risk of serious harm to others.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman attends repeatedly with minor injuries. Her boyfriend always accompanies her, answers for her, and refuses to leave the cubicle. What is the best way to obtain a private history?

options.text: Explain that a part of every assessment is done alone and ask him to wait outside
Tell him you suspect he is hurting her
Ask about abuse in front of him but in vague language
Skip the history and treat the injury only

questions.correctOptionText: Explain that a part of every assessment is done alone and ask him to wait outside

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a routine reason to separate avoids accusing him and protects the patient.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: confronting him is dangerous for the patient.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: vague wording in his presence prevents honest disclosure and may alert him.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this misses a chance to identify and support someone at risk.

questions.explanation: Presenting separation as routine practice lets you create privacy without revealing your concern. Confrontation or asking in his presence risks retaliation after she leaves.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with a severe learning disability, who lacks capacity to decide about sharing information, has repeated fingertip-pattern bruises on her arms. She attends a day centre, and a particular support worker is always present when she is distressed. Which statement best describes your confidentiality position if you raise the concern?

options.text: Sharing the minimum necessary information with the safeguarding team is justified in his best interests
You must obtain the support worker's consent first
You must not share anything because he cannot consent
You should share her whole medical record with the day centre manager

questions.correctOptionText: Sharing the minimum necessary information with the safeguarding team is justified in his best interests

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lack of capacity means acting in best interests under the Mental Capacity Act, sharing only what is needed.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the support worker is a possible abuser and their consent is neither required nor appropriate.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: lacking capacity does not prevent best-interests disclosure to protect the person.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: disclosure must be proportionate and limited to those who need to know.

questions.explanation: For an adult who lacks capacity, decisions including disclosure are made in their best interests under the Mental Capacity Act 2005. Information is shared proportionately with the safeguarding team and not widely, and the reasons are documented.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with early Parkinson's disease is cared for at home by her husband, who has recently begun refusing to let her see friends, controls her bank card, and calls her 'useless' in front of others. Name the forms of abuse this may represent and explain why recognition can be difficult.
markingGuide: Identifies psychological or emotional abuse (humiliation, isolation)
Identifies financial or material abuse (controlling money)
Recognises coercive control as part of domestic abuse
States that abuse is often hidden because of dependency, loyalty, fear or shame
States that the patient may not disclose and that concern is built from the whole picture
questions.explanation: Isolation from friends and humiliation are psychological abuse, control of her bank card is financial abuse, and the whole pattern is coercive control within domestic abuse. Dependence on the abuser, loyalty and fear make disclosure unlikely, so professionals must notice patterns rather than wait for a complaint.

questions.stem: Describe the conditions under which a doctor may share confidential information about an adult with capacity without their consent, and what safeguards should apply when doing so.
markingGuide: Seek consent first and respect refusal as the default for an adult with capacity
Disclosure justified when required by law or court order
Disclosure justified in the public interest to prevent a risk of death or serious harm to the person or others
Share only the minimum information necessary with those who need it
Tell the patient before disclosure unless that would increase risk
Document the decision and the reasoning
questions.explanation: Confidentiality is a strong duty but not absolute: the law and a serious risk of harm to others can justify disclosure. Proportionality, informing the patient where safe and clear documentation are the safeguards that make the disclosure defensible.

questions.stem: After a woman with capacity discloses abuse in a private consultation, which of the following is the most appropriate documentation?

options.text: A factual record of her account in her own words, with the actions agreed, stored where the partner cannot see it
A note stating that she is 'a victim of domestic violence by her husband' without further detail
No record in case it is later seen by the abuser
A letter posted to her home summarising the disclosure

questions.correctOptionText: A factual record of her account in her own words, with the actions agreed, stored where the partner cannot see it

distractorRationale.a: Correct: factual, attributed and securely stored, with agreed safe contact arrangements.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: it records a conclusion rather than the facts and her words.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: failing to document undermines care, safeguarding and any later legal process.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: posting to the home may be intercepted and put her at risk.

questions.explanation: Good documentation records what was said and seen, not conclusions, and is kept where an abuser cannot read it. Communication with the patient should use methods she has agreed are safe.

questions.stem: If you suspect abuse of an adult at risk, you should investigate it fully yourself before involving anyone else.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: You are expected to recognise and escalate concerns, not to investigate or prove abuse. Escalate to your supervisor and the named safeguarding lead promptly, following local policy.
